description: We are people from Lumen Space Academy (Tashkent)
summary: LUMEN Skywatch is a free web game that turns anyone into a sky hunter using real data from NASA’s SPHEREx and WISE missions. In 10 minutes, 5 training levels on real WISE frames teach the blink method that found Pluto: spotting what moves, telling real objects from glitches, reading chemistry from spectra and checking the catalogue. Players then solve NASA’s five test cases on live SPHEREx data and explore any patch of sky by coordinates or name. For every object the tool measures motion and brightness changes, flags signs of water, methane, CO₂ and CO across SPHEREx’s infrared bands, and checks SIMBAD and Gaia, so a new find becomes a candidate with a report. On NASA’s test objects it gives five correct verdicts and measures proper motion within 7% of catalogue values. It works in English, Russian and Uzbek, so a student in Central Asia can join the search on a phone
details:
What it does. LUMEN Skywatch answers the challenge directly: a user enters a sky position (RA/Dec or an object name) and sees a short animation of SPHEREx images of that patch over time, making moving and changing objects easy to spot. On top of that core we built three layers.

1. Training (levels 1–5). Real WISE/NEOWISE frames (2010–2024) teach one skill per level: the blink method, a real mover vs. a planted glitch, slow drift over years, reading ices from a spectrum, and checking a find against the catalogue. The final exam asks players to find a real brown dwarf (Gliese 570 D) without hints.

2. NASA's test cases (levels 6–10). Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis become detective cases on live SPHEREx data. The tool's results: Barnard's Star 9.91″/yr (catalogue 10.39″/yr), WISE 0855 7.62″/yr (8.15″/yr), Epsilon Indi B 4.39″/yr (4.68″/yr); RW Aurigae and R Draconis are correctly flagged as variable stars with steady positions.

3. Free exploration. Any coordinates or name, curated "Surprise me" fields, a choice of field of view, all six SPHEREx detector arrays, a switch between SPHEREx and the long WISE baseline, Blink / What changed / Trail modes, and four molecule lenses. Clicking an object opens a card with its measured motion and direction, brightness variability, molecular signs, an on-the-fly spectrum and a SIMBAD/Gaia match. Unmatched movers become candidates and can be filed as field reports. Sky positions are encoded in the URL, so any view can be shared or embedded.

How it works. A Python/FastAPI backend finds SPHEREx Level 2 exposures covering a position, cuts out the region, groups exposures by sky pass and detector, reprojects them onto a common grid and stacks them per epoch. Image files are read directly from NASA's open AWS bucket; IRSA is used to search for exposures, and when it is unavailable the backend switches to our own coverage index, built from the headers of the files in that bucket. Motion is measured from centroid positions across epochs; variability from aperture photometry; the spectrum from each exposure's wavelength at the object's position; molecular signs from band depths relative to the neighbouring continuum. The frontend is a single HTML/JavaScript page with no login.

Benefits and intended impact. SPHEREx images more than a billion objects, far more than professionals can inspect, and most known brown dwarfs and comets were found by volunteers. LUMEN Skywatch lowers the entry bar to ten minutes and zero prior knowledge, so many more people can help. It also saves volunteers' time: each object comes with an instant answer to "how fast does it move, what is it made of, and is it already known?", so effort goes to real candidates instead of known stars and artefacts. Because the interface is in English, Russian and Uzbek and runs on a phone, it opens NASA data to students in Central Asia, a region rarely reached by citizen-science projects. We plan to use it with school students in Uzbekistan as their first hands-on contact with real space data.

How it is creative. Most blink tools stop at "something moved". We combine two NASA missions for two different jobs: WISE's 14-year baseline to catch slow motion, and SPHEREx's 102 infrared bands to read chemistry, turned into simple "molecule lenses" anyone can switch on. Instead of a manual, the tool teaches through a game: levels, detective cases, ranks and a final exam on a real brown dwarf. The first level gives a newcomer the same experience that led to Pluto's discovery, in about ten seconds.

Factors we considered.

  • Scientific honesty: molecular results are labelled as signs, not proof; we validated motion and variability against SIMBAD and Gaia on NASA's five test objects before trusting them.
  • SPHEREx specifics: each exposure sees a different wavelength across the detector, so we compare and stack images per detector and per sky pass to avoid false "motion".
  • Small motions: nearby stars move only a few SPHEREx pixels per year, so the tool measures centroids and adds the long WISE baseline.
  • Reliability: the app keeps working when the IRSA archive is down, using our own index of the open AWS files.
  • Accessibility: no login, works on phones, three languages, plain-language explanations and hints.
  • Speed: adjustable field of view and caching, because archive searches can be slow.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, NumPy, SciPy, photutils, reproject, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Railway hosting; Anthropic's Claude via Claude Code
